citeAs: Yuzhen Huang, Yuzhuo Bai, Zhihao Zhu, Junlei Zhang, Jinghan Zhang, Tangjun Su, Junteng Liu, Chuancheng Lv, Yikai Zhang, Jiayi Lei, Yao Fu, Maosong Sun, Junxian He (2023). C-Eval: A Multi-Level Multi-Discipline Chinese Evaluation Suite for Foundation Models. 37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2023) Track on Datasets and Benchmarks.
creator: Yuzhen Huang, Yuzhuo Bai, Zhihao Zhu, Junlei Zhang, Jinghan Zhang, Tangjun Su, Junteng Liu, Chuancheng Lv, Yikai Zhang, Jiayi Lei, Yao Fu, Maosong Sun, Junxian He (Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Tsinghua University, University of Edinburgh, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology)
description: C-Eval is the first comprehensive Chinese evaluation suite designed to assess advanced knowledge and reasoning abilities of foundation models in a Chinese context. It comprises 13,948 multiple-choice questions across 52 diverse disciplines (ranging from humanities to science and engineering) at four difficulty levels: middle school, high school, college, and professional. It is accompanied by C-Eval HARD, a subset of particularly challenging subjects requiring advanced reasoning abilities.
name: C-Eval
publisher: HKUST NLP Group (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology)
rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotation was performed by the paper's authors, who are researchers affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Tsinghua University, University of Edinburgh, and The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. No further demographic details are provided.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Manual annotation was performed directly by the authors (no external crowdsourcing platform mentioned).
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Questions underwent several rounds of human validation by the authors. For the development split, five exemplars per subject were annotated with step-by-step explanations to enable few-shot chain-of-thought evaluation. Explanations were first automatically generated by prompting GPT-4, then manually revised by the authors (Yuzhen Huang, Yuzhuo Bai, and Junxian He) to obtain final high-quality explanations.
rai:dataBiases: The paper acknowledges that English benchmarks tend to exhibit geographical biases towards the domestic knowledge of the regions that produce them, which motivated the creation of C-Eval for Chinese contexts. To mitigate data contamination/leakage bias, questions were collected from mock exams or small-scale local exams (rather than official national exams), and mostly sourced from PDF or Word documents rather than plain text, to reduce the risk of questions being included in LLM pretraining data. The paper also notes that there are fluctuations in the distribution of correct answer options (A: 22.9%, B: 26.0%, C: 26.4%, D: 24.7%), though these are described as relatively small and similar to MMLU.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected from mock exams and small-scale local exams freely available on the internet (primarily as PDF or Microsoft Word documents, and a minor fraction as web pages), as well as past exam questions from top universities in China publicly shared by students. A minor fraction of college questions are mock questions for the national graduate entrance exam sourced from the Weipu website, for which authorization was obtained to include around 2000 such questions. Questions were collected across four difficulty levels (middle school, high school, college, professional) spanning 52 disciplines.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consists of mock exam questions and past exam questions collected primarily from PDF and Microsoft Word documents available on the internet, as well as a minor fraction from web pages. A portion of college-level questions came from past exam papers from top Chinese universities shared by students, and approximately 2000 questions from the Weipu website (national graduate entrance exam mock questions).
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataLimitations: The authors acknowledge that C-Eval, along with all English-language benchmarks, is far from perfect for LLM evaluation. Many other abilities such as reasoning over and calling APIs are not covered, and multiple aspects beyond accuracy — including safety, bias, and robustness — are not assessed. The benchmark uses only multiple-choice format, which is a proxy for advanced abilities. There is also a risk of data contamination since exam questions from national tests may be present in LLM pretraining data, though steps were taken to mitigate this.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: PDF documents were initially processed into text. All questions were subsequently parsed — automatically when possible, and otherwise manually by the authors — into a structured format. For subjects with complex mathematical notations (e.g., STEM subjects), equations were manually converted into standard LaTeX formats. All questions were processed to include exactly four choices: questions with fewer than four options were eliminated, and incorrect choices were randomly dropped for questions with more than four options. Questions also went through a standard data preprocessing pipeline including deduplication and cleaning. All LaTeX notations were ensured to compile without syntax errors. Questions were randomly split into development, validation, and test sets within each subject (validation and test at a 1:9 ratio), with at least around 200 questions processed per subject.
rai:dataSocialImpact: C-Eval is intended to foster the development and growth of foundation models for Chinese users. It addresses the gap between Chinese LLM development and evaluation, providing a benchmark that reflects Chinese cultural, historical, and legal knowledge rather than relying on translated English benchmarks. The authors note that LLM evaluation should transcend casual conversational bots and guide developers in preparing LLMs for more complex scenarios.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluating advanced knowledge and reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs) / foundation models in a Chinese context. Intended to help developers understand model abilities from multiple dimensions, identify strengths and shortcomings, and guide improvement. Can be used as a whole suite or as subsets to assess specific model abilities. Supports zero-shot and few-shot evaluation in both answer-only and chain-of-thought settings.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: GPT-4 was used to automatically generate step-by-step chain-of-thought explanations for the development split exemplars, which were then manually revised by the authors.

null_reasons.rai:annotationsPerItem: The paper does not specify a number of independent annotations collected per item; validation was done through cross-validation rounds by the authors collectively.
null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: No inter-annotator agreement metrics or formal annotation quality analysis are reported in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper does not discuss missing data handling in the collection process.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: No specific timeframe or date range for data collection is mentioned in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation of missing values is described; not applicable to this exam question dataset.
null_reasons.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: No post-collection augmentation, balancing, or resampling of the dataset itself is described beyond the preprocessing steps already captured.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No versioning, update cadence, or maintenance plan is described in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset consists of exam questions and does not contain personal or sensitive information about individuals.
